rows.source: UKHSA tuberculosis screening and public-health control
rows.verified: UKHSA tuberculosis resources cover diagnosis, screening, treatment, prevention, epidemiology and surveillance.

rows.source: UKHSA tuberculosis screening and public-health control
rows.verified: Tuberculosis is a notifiable disease in the UK and diagnosed cases should be notified to the local UKHSA Health Protection Team.

rows.source: UKHSA tuberculosis screening and public-health control
rows.verified: Contacts of identified TB cases are traced, screened and treated as appropriate.

rows.source: UKHSA tuberculosis screening and public-health control
rows.verified: Local health protection teams become involved where congregate settings, clusters or outbreaks are identified.

rows.source: UKHSA tuberculosis screening and public-health control
rows.verified: Primary care should maintain vigilance, educate at-risk patients and promptly refer suspected active TB.

rows.source: UKHSA tuberculosis screening and public-health control
rows.verified: UK pre-entry TB screening must be performed by a recognised and quality-assured provider.

rows.source: UKHSA tuberculosis screening and public-health control
rows.verified: Pre-entry screening detects active pulmonary TB at the time of screening but does not replace eligible latent-TB screening after arrival.

rows.source: UKHSA tuberculosis screening and public-health control
rows.verified: UKHSA has reviewed evidence on contact-tracing strategies for people exposed to active TB in low-incidence countries.

rows.source: UKHSA tuberculosis screening and public-health control
rows.verified: Tuberculosis risk depends on infectiousness, duration and setting of exposure, ventilation, organism, immunity, screening, treatment and adherence.

rows.source: UKHSA tuberculosis screening and public-health control
rows.verified: UKHSA tuberculosis evidence is case-, contact-, setting-, screening-, treatment- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.

rows.source: OPSS baby self-feeding product safety
rows.verified: OPSS classifies baby self-feeding products as presenting a serious risk of harm or death.

rows.source: OPSS baby self-feeding product safety
rows.verified: Self-feeding pillows can cause choking when liquid is delivered faster than a baby can swallow.

rows.source: OPSS baby self-feeding product safety
rows.verified: Baby self-feeding products can cause aspiration pneumonia when feed enters the airway.

rows.source: OPSS baby self-feeding product safety
rows.verified: The design and intended use create risks that cannot be mitigated by instructions.

rows.source: OPSS baby self-feeding product safety
rows.verified: Consumers are advised to stop using baby self-feeding products immediately and dispose of them safely.

rows.source: OPSS baby self-feeding product safety
rows.verified: Businesses must remove baby self-feeding products from the market and comply with product-safety law.

rows.source: OPSS baby self-feeding product safety
rows.verified: A 2026 recall identified a hands-free baby self-feeding pillow as a serious choking and aspiration risk.

rows.source: OPSS baby self-feeding product safety
rows.verified: OPSS states that the category is inherently dangerous because the infant cannot control feed flow or respond effectively to choking.

rows.source: OPSS baby self-feeding product safety
rows.verified: Baby self-feeding risk depends on product design, feed flow, infant age and ability, position, supervision, use duration and response time.

rows.source: OPSS baby self-feeding product safety
rows.verified: OPSS self-feeding-product evidence is product-, infant-, use-, exposure-, clinical- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
